lines: Okay, review. Who actually reads these specs?

Fewer people than you'd hope. Most tool users skim specs, or hand the review to another agent. Adversarial review by a second model, or asking an LLM to find gaps. Full human review showed up mainly where the organization made it a team activity, with product managers, senior engineers, and tech leads involved.
And the repos back that up?

Starkly. Ninety-eight point three percent of spec files with a recorded history have a single author. Of the inline pull request comments on specs, sixty-eight and a half percent were written by bots. And two hundred ten of the two hundred sixty-six repos had no inline comments on specs at all.
To be fair, the authors are careful here. Review can happen in Slack or in a meeting and never show up in Git.

True. But code verification tells a similar story. Nearly everyone verifies through tests the agent wrote. One participant said none of those tests are written by hand. Another called the result verification debt.
That's a phrase product owners should write on a whiteboard.

Then retention. Practitioners split three ways. Some keep a living spec that's updated as the system changes. Some keep an accumulated change record: a new spec for every change, and nothing deleted. A few throw specs away after implementation and keep intent in tickets or tests.

Eighty-one and a half percent of spec files have exactly one recorded commit. Written once, then never touched again. In OpenSpec repos, archived change specs outnumber the living capability specs about three to one. Commit counts do understate revision somewhat, because renames break history, but the pattern is clear.
